paragraphs: Rocks that form from cooling lava record the direction of Earth's magnetic field at the moment they solidify, because tiny magnetic grains in the melt align with the field and are locked in place. When geologists examined sequences of such rocks, they found that the recorded direction was not constant: layers laid down at different times pointed in nearly opposite directions. The most straightforward explanation is that the field itself has reversed polarity many times in Earth's history.

Not everyone accepted this at first. Some argued that certain minerals can spontaneously acquire a magnetization opposite to that of the surrounding field, so that reversed rocks might say nothing about the field at all. The decisive evidence was that rocks of the same age, from widely separated continents and made of different minerals, showed the same pattern of reversals. A chemical quirk of one mineral could hardly account for a pattern shared across so many kinds of rock, and the field-reversal explanation became the accepted one.
